title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

refs.capture: p.936 left column, lower half: the single paragraph under the heading 'Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease' (starts 'Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)…', ends with the sentence about women's smoking).

basics: Air moves only because of a pressure difference, and the flow you get for a given pressure difference falls steeply as an airway narrows (flow = pressure difference / resistance; resistance rises with the fourth power of shrinking radius). 'Obstructive' disease therefore means the patient cannot push air OUT fast enough: airways are narrowed by mucus and inflammation, or they collapse during exhalation because the elastic tissue that normally holds them open has been destroyed. COPD is the umbrella term for two overlapping conditions with the same main cause, long-term inhaled irritants (mostly cigarette smoke): emphysema (destroyed alveolar walls, lost recoil) and chronic bronchitis (chronically inflamed, mucus-clogged bronchi). Spirometry measures the limitation as a reduced FEV1. The slide leaves unsaid that COPD is largely irreversible (unlike asthma), that it is one of the leading causes of death, and that it is mostly preventable.

terms.d: Opposition to airflow offered by the airways; depends mainly on bronchiolar diameter, which smooth muscle and swelling can change.
Tiny thin-walled air sac at the end of the airway tree where gas exchange with blood happens.
Small airway (under about 1 mm) with smooth muscle but no cartilage, so it can narrow or collapse.
Permanent destruction of alveolar walls, giving large air spaces and loss of elastic recoil.
Long-standing inflammation of the bronchi with excess mucus and a productive cough.
Harmful or irritating to tissue, e.g. smoke, dust, chemical fumes.
Measuring the volumes of air breathed in and out with a spirometer.
Volume forcibly exhaled in the first second after a maximal inhalation; falls when airways are obstructed.

refs.capture: p.914 right column: the paragraph under the run-in heading 'Exhalation' (starts 'Breathing out, called exhalation…'), which explains elastic recoil. p.915 right column: the paragraph under the run-in heading 'Compliance of the Lungs' (one paragraph; its last sentence is about emphysema).

basics: A healthy lung behaves like a stretched elastic bag: inhalation stretches it, and it springs back by itself, which is all that drives quiet exhalation. The recoil comes from elastic fibres in the alveolar walls and from surface tension in the alveolar fluid. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, so two things happen: the gas-exchange surface shrinks (less oxygen uptake, breathlessness on exertion, low arterial oxygen) and elastic fibres are lost, so the lung becomes floppy (high compliance) and fails to empty. Air is trapped, residual volume and total lung capacity rise, and the over-inflated chest becomes barrel-shaped. Small airways have no cartilage; they are held open by the surrounding elastic tissue, so without it they collapse when the patient forces air out, which is why FEV1 drops. Breathing out through pursed lips keeps pressure inside the airways higher and delays that collapse. The book explains the mechanism but not the acinar subtypes.

terms.d: Last purely conducting airway; everything distal to it (respiratory bronchioles, ducts, alveoli) exchanges gas.
The unit of lung tissue supplied by one terminal bronchiole; 'centriacinar' and 'panacinar' describe which part is destroyed.
Tendency of stretched lung tissue and chest wall to spring back, powering quiet exhalation.
How easily the lungs stretch for a given pressure change; high compliance = floppy, low = stiff.
All the air the lungs can hold after a maximal inhalation (vital capacity plus residual volume).
Air left in the lungs after the most forceful exhalation; it cannot be measured by spirometry.
Volume exhaled in the first second of a forced exhalation; reduced when airways collapse or narrow.
Subjective difficulty or labour in breathing; shortness of breath.
Abnormally low partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood.
Mucus and fluid coughed up from the airways.

basics: A chest radiograph is a shadow picture: X-rays pass easily through air, so air-filled lung looks black, while bone, heart and fluid absorb them and look white. The 'interstitium' is the fine scaffolding between the air sacs, the connective tissue with elastic and reticular fibres, small blood vessels and lymphatics that Tortora draws around the alveoli in Figures 23.11 and 23.12; when it is thickened or distorted it shows as extra fine lines on the film. In emphysema the lungs are overfilled with trapped air, so the lung fields look longer and darker than normal. The diaphragm is a dome that flattens as it contracts during inhalation; a chronically over-inflated lung pushes it down so that on the film both halves (hemidiaphragms) look flat even at rest, instead of domed. Reading these signs assumes you already know what a normal chest X-ray looks like and how lung inflation is produced.

basics: The airways are lined by a mucous membrane: a surface epithelium (ciliated columnar cells plus mucus-secreting goblet cells) sitting on a basement membrane, over loose connective tissue (lamina propria) and a submucosa containing mucous glands, blood vessels and, deeper, smooth muscle and cartilage. Mucus traps inhaled particles and the cilia sweep it up to the throat. Years of inhaled irritant make the glands enlarge (hypertrophy) and the goblet cells multiply (hyperplasia), so mucus is produced faster than it can be cleared: the definition of chronic bronchitis is a productive cough for at least three months in two consecutive years. Plugs of mucus block airflow, so alveoli behind them are poorly ventilated; oxygen falls and carbon dioxide rises in the blood, producing cyanosis (blue-tinged skin from de-oxygenated haemoglobin). Poorly ventilated lung regions also constrict their blood vessels, which raises pulmonary artery pressure and eventually strains the right heart. The micrograph on the slide shows exactly these layers, inflamed.

terms.d: Epithelium plus underlying loose connective tissue lining a passage open to the outside, e.g. the airways.
Mucus-secreting epithelial cell shaped like a wine glass, scattered among ciliated cells.

basics: Asthma is an allergic-type (type I hypersensitivity) inflammation of the bronchi. The adaptive immune system normally reacts to foreign proteins (antigens) by presenting them to helper T cells; a T-helper-2 pattern of response makes B cells switch to producing IgE antibody, which docks on mast cells in the airway lining. The next time the allergen arrives it bridges two IgE molecules and the mast cell 'degranulates', dumping histamine, leukotrienes and other mediators. Within minutes these contract the bronchial smooth muscle (bronchioles have no cartilage, so they narrow), make capillaries leak (oedema) and drive mucus secretion; nerve reflexes through the vagus add to the constriction. Hours later, chemokines such as IL-5 recruit eosinophils and other leukocytes, whose granule proteins strip the epithelium and leave the airway hyper-reactive. Because the muscle spasm and swelling can relax, the obstruction is reversible, which distinguishes asthma from COPD. Tortora gives the two-phase picture and mediators; the cytokine cascade is the lecturer's addition.

terms.d: An immune response that is excessive or misdirected and damages the body's own tissues.
An otherwise harmless antigen (pollen, dust-mite protein) that triggers an allergic reaction in sensitised people.
Antigen-presenting cell that captures foreign material and shows fragments of it to T cells.
CD4 lymphocyte that coordinates immune responses by secreting cytokines; Th2 cells favour antibody and allergic responses.
A cytokine, a signalling protein passed between white blood cells (e.g. IL-4 drives IgE production).
The antibody class that binds mast cells and basophils and mediates allergic reactions.
Cell-surface protein that grips the constant 'tail' of an antibody, holding it on the cell.
Connective-tissue cell packed with histamine granules; releases them when its bound IgE is cross-linked.
Granular white blood cell prominent in allergy and parasite defence; its granule proteins damage epithelium.
Parasympathetic reflex via the vagus nerve; in the airways it causes bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion.

note: Th2, eotaxin, major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein are not in Tortora. Tortora's Table 22.2 says IL-4 causes plasma cells to secrete IgE; it assigns IgA (not eosinophil recruitment) to IL-5.

refs.section_title: Regulation of bronchiolar smooth muscle (sympathetic vs parasympathetic)
refs.capture: p.905 right column, top: the two paragraphs starting 'patency. basics: The calibre of a bronchiole is set by its smooth muscle, which has two remote controls: the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal adrenaline relax it (bronchodilation, acting through beta-2 receptors), while the parasympathetic vagus nerve, histamine and cold or irritant stimulation contract it. Anything that tips this balance toward contraction, or that inflames an already twitchy airway, can start an attack. That is the logic of the trigger list: allergens act through IgE and mast cells; viral infections and pollutants inflame the mucosa; cold dry air and hard exercise irritate the airway directly; emotional stress works through the autonomic nerves. The drug examples follow too: beta-blockers remove the sympathetic 'relax' signal, and aspirin-type NSAIDs shift arachidonic-acid metabolism toward bronchoconstricting leukotrienes in susceptible people. Tortora names most of the triggers but explains only the autonomic mechanism; it does not mention beta-blockers or viral infections.

terms.d: Extrinsic = external allergen-driven; intrinsic = non-allergic causes such as infection, exercise or drugs.
The 'fight or flight' part of the autonomic nervous system; relaxes airway smooth muscle.
The 'rest and digest' part; via the vagus it constricts airways and stimulates mucus.

basics: The airways branch about 23 times from the trachea to the alveolar ducts, so anything that solidifies inside them takes the shape of a tree. In a severe attack the mucus produced by the inflamed lining becomes thick, sticky and full of shed cells, and can set into a cast that plugs a whole bronchus; the spiral-shaped plugs come from mucus moulded inside narrowed, twisted bronchioles. Wheeze is the whistling sound air makes when it is forced through a narrowed tube, loudest on breathing out because airways narrow further during exhalation. Dyspnoea is the sensation of not getting enough air. 'Status asthmaticus' is an attack that does not respond to the usual bronchodilators and is life-threatening because the plugs and spasm block ventilation of large parts of the lung. Tortora describes the mucus clogging and lists the symptoms; the cast and the term status asthmaticus are the lecturer's.

basics: Each lung sits inside a double serous membrane: visceral pleura on the lung, parietal pleura on the chest wall, a thin film of fluid between. There is no air in this pleural 'cavity', and its pressure is always a few mmHg below atmospheric, so the lung, which would otherwise shrink by its own elastic recoil, is held out against the chest wall by suction, much as two wet glass slides cling together. If air gets in, from outside through a chest wound or from inside through a burst weak spot (bleb) on the lung surface, the suction is lost and the lung collapses (atelectasis). Because the two pleural sacs are separate, the other lung keeps working. Air under pressure can push the mediastinum (heart and great vessels) toward the other side. A chest tube removes the air so the lung re-expands. Tortora covers the mechanism, atelectasis and the chest tube, not the spontaneous/traumatic split or mediastinal shift.

terms.d: Two-layered serous membrane: visceral layer on the lung, parietal layer on the thoracic wall.
The potential space between the two pleural layers, normally containing only a film of fluid.

basics: Pneumonia is infection with inflammation of the gas-exchange part of the lung. Microbes that get past the mucus-and-cilia defences multiply in the alveoli; the immune response makes capillaries leak, and the alveoli fill with fluid, cells and pus instead of air, so gas exchange fails in that region. Fluid-filled lung absorbs X-rays, so it appears as a white shadow on a chest radiograph, which is the main diagnostic picture; identifying the organism in sputum or blood guides antibiotic choice. The classification on the slide is anatomical: 'lobar' pneumonia fills a whole lobe (each lobe has its own lobar bronchus, and the right lung has three lobes, the left two); 'bronchopneumonia' is patchy, spreading from many small bronchi into their lobules; 'interstitial' pneumonia inflames the alveolar walls and connective-tissue scaffold rather than filling the air spaces, and is typical of viruses. Tortora explains the disease and its commonest cause (Streptococcus pneumoniae) but not the three patterns.

terms.d: A major division of a lung marked off by a fissure; three on the right, two on the left.

basics: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slow-growing bacterium that survives inside the very macrophages sent to eat it. The body's answer is cell-mediated (T-cell) immunity: T cells activate macrophages, which surround the bacteria in a nodule (granuloma) whose centre dies into a cheese-like ('caseous') mass; this heals by fibrosis and calcification, leaving a small scar in the lung plus a scarred draining lymph node, the Ghon complex of primary infection. The bacteria can stay dormant for life. If immunity later falls (age, HIV, malnutrition), they reactivate, characteristically in the upper lobes near the apex where ventilation exceeds blood flow so oxygen is plentiful and lymph drainage sluggish; cavities form and bacteria may spill into the bloodstream, seeding 'miliary' (millet-seed) foci throughout the lungs or other organs. Tortora gives the immune walling-off, dormancy and reactivation story and the symptoms, but not the granuloma histology, Ghon complex, apical preference or miliary spread.

terms.d: Genus of slow-growing bacteria with a waxy cell wall; M. tuberculosis causes TB.

refs.capture: p.905 left column: numbered item 1 of the structural changes list (epithelium types from main bronchi to terminal bronchioles).

basics: A cancer is a population of cells that has acquired DNA mutations letting it divide without control, invade neighbouring tissue and seed distant sites (metastasis) via lymph and blood. Carcinogens in cigarette tar cause most of these mutations in the airway lining, which is why 85% of lung cancers occur in smokers; asbestos and silica dust add to the risk. Because the lung has few pain nerves, early tumours are silent; cough, breathlessness and weight loss appear late. Nearly all lung cancers are carcinomas (epithelial), named by the cell type they resemble: adenocarcinoma from gland-like or alveolar cells, usually peripheral; squamous-cell carcinoma from the flattened cells of larger bronchi, central; small-cell carcinoma from neuroendocrine cells near the hilum, fast-spreading; large-cell when undifferentiated. Staging uses the TNM system, scoring the tumour's size, lymph-node spread and metastases to guide treatment. Tortora covers causes, types and symptoms but not TNM staging or the percentage breakdown.

basics: The heart is two pumps side by side: the left drives the high-resistance systemic circuit at about 120 mmHg, the right the low-resistance lungs at roughly a quarter of that. Any abnormal opening between the two sides therefore lets blood flow from left to right, from high pressure to low, so oxygenated blood is recirculated through the lungs. Before birth such openings are normal: the foramen ovale (between the atria) and the ductus arteriosus (pulmonary trunk to aorta) bypass the unused fetal lungs and should seal after the first breaths. An atrial septal defect is a foramen ovale (or septum) that fails to close; a ventricular septal defect is an incomplete interventricular septum; a patent ductus is the fetal vessel staying open. In each, the lungs receive extra flow; over years their vessels thicken, pulmonary pressure rises, and the right ventricle is overloaded. Tortora describes the defects and fetal shunts but only hints at the pulmonary-hypertension consequence.

terms.d: An abnormal passage letting blood bypass its normal route; left-to-right means oxygenated blood re-enters the pulmonary side.
The muscular wall separating the two atria or the two ventricles.
Fetal opening in the interatrial septum; normally closes at birth leaving the fossa ovalis.

The artery leaving the right ventricle that splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries.

basics: Blood is only oxygenated if it passes through the lungs; a right-to-left shunt sends some de-oxygenated blood straight from the right heart into the aorta, so the arterial blood carries a lot of haemoglobin without oxygen, which is dark bluish-red and shows through skin and lips as cyanosis. For blood to move right-to-left the pressure on the right must be raised above the left, and that is what the tetralogy of Fallot does: a narrowed right-ventricular outflow (pulmonary stenosis) blocks the easy route to the lungs, so the right ventricle thickens (hypertrophy) and pushes blood through the ventricular septal defect into an aorta that sits astride the defect and receives blood from both ventricles. In transposition, the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left, so the two circuits run in parallel and survival depends on some mixing (e.g. a patent ductus). Tortora explains the tetralogy and cyanosis; transposition is not in the book.

basics: An artery wall has three coats: intima (endothelial cells on a basement membrane, bounded by an elastic sheet), media (smooth muscle and elastic fibres) and externa (connective tissue). Cholesterol travels in the blood in lipoprotein particles; the low-density type (LDL) delivers it to cells. When the endothelium is injured by high pressure, smoke chemicals or excess LDL, LDL leaks into the intima and is oxidised. Oxidised LDL is treated as foreign: monocytes enter, become macrophages, gorge on it and turn into 'foam cells'; T cells amplify the inflammation. Smooth-muscle cells migrate in from the media and lay down collagen, forming a fibrous cap over a core of dead foam cells and lipid, which later calcifies. The plaque narrows the lumen; if its cap cracks, a clot forms and can block the vessel outright. Risk rises with hypertension, high cholesterol, age and male sex. Tortora gives the whole sequence, noting that most heart attacks follow cap rupture rather than gradual narrowing.

basics: This slide retells the previous one step by step, so the key is the artery wall's anatomy. Blood touches only the endothelium; beneath it lies the thin intima, then a fenestrated sheet of elastin (the internal elastic membrane), then the thick smooth-muscle media. Endothelial cells are not a passive lining: when injured they become 'sticky', displaying adhesion molecules that catch passing monocytes and T cells, and leaky, letting LDL through. Inside the intima, LDL is oxidised by free radicals and becomes a target for macrophages, which engulf it until they are foam cells. Cytokines and growth factors from foam cells and T cells then summon smooth-muscle cells, which squeeze through the holes of the internal elastic membrane, multiply in the intima and switch from contracting to secreting collagen. That collagen cap walls the lipid pool and dead cells off from the blood: a mature plaque, which can grow outward for decades before it narrows the lumen.

basics: The aorta is the body's main pressure vessel: a 2–3 cm elastic tube that takes the full force of each left-ventricular beat, stretching in systole and recoiling in diastole. It is described in four segments: ascending aorta, arch, thoracic (descending, in the chest) and abdominal (below the diaphragm), so an aneurysm is classified by which segment bulges. The wall is strong because its media is layered elastin and smooth muscle; if that media degenerates (atherosclerosis, ageing, inherited connective-tissue weakness, infection such as syphilis), the wall can no longer resist the pressure and stretches into a local balloon. By Laplace's law wall tension rises with radius, so the wider the sac the faster it grows and the likelier it is to tear or burst, producing catastrophic internal bleeding. Tortora defines aneurysm only briefly in Medical Terminology; the segment-based classification and the wall-weakness mechanism are inferred from the aorta and elastic-artery anatomy.

basics: Heart muscle cannot take oxygen from the blood inside its own chambers; it is fed by the two coronary arteries that leave the aorta just above the aortic valve and run in the grooves of the heart surface. Cardiac muscle works continuously and almost entirely aerobically, so it needs a steady oxygen supply. When an atherosclerotic plaque narrows a coronary artery, supply may be adequate at rest but not during exertion: the muscle becomes hypoxic, releases pain-producing metabolites, and the patient feels a crushing chest pain (angina) that eases with rest. Coronary branches do connect with each other (anastomoses), so a slowly narrowing vessel can be partly bypassed by collateral flow. If a plaque ruptures and a clot blocks the artery completely, the muscle downstream dies within hours: myocardial infarction. Dead muscle is replaced by non-contracting scar, weakening the pump, and if the infarct involves the conduction system it can trigger fatal ventricular fibrillation.

basics: The heart wall has three layers: the endocardium lining the chambers, the thick myocardium, and the epicardium outside. Coronary arteries run on the outer surface and send branches inward, so the innermost third of the myocardium (the subendocardium) is the last to be perfused and the first to suffer when flow drops; it is also squeezed hardest by the pressure inside the ventricle during systole. The slide sorts infarcts by which vessel problem produces which pattern. A partial or temporary block of one coronary artery, or one that is reopened early by clot-busting drugs or angioplasty, kills only the subendocardium in that artery's territory (regional subendocardial). Severe shock, meaning arterial pressure too low to perfuse any of the inner wall, kills the subendocardium all the way round the left ventricle (circumferential). Tiny scattered infarcts follow blockage of small intramural branches by emboli, vessel inflammation or spasm. Tortora covers infarction, reperfusion damage and shock, but not this pattern classification.

basics: The heartbeat is an electrical event first: a cluster of self-firing cells, the SA node in the right atrium, depolarises about 70–75 times a minute, the wave spreads through the atria, is delayed at the AV node (so the atria finish contracting before the ventricles start), then races down the AV bundle (bundle of His), its branches and the Purkinje fibres to fire both ventricles together. An arrhythmia is any fault in this system. Rate faults: tachycardia (too fast) and bradycardia (too slow). Conduction faults: heart block, where the AV node or bundle delays (first-degree), drops some beats (second-degree) or transmits nothing so the ventricles fall back on their own slow escape pacemaker (complete block). Coordination faults: fibrillation, where fibres fire chaotically and the chamber only quivers. Atrial fibrillation is survivable because the ventricles still pump, but stagnant atrial blood clots and can embolise to the brain; ventricular fibrillation stops all output and is fatal within minutes unless defibrillated.

basics: An ECG records, from electrodes on the skin, the tiny voltages produced as waves of depolarisation and repolarisation sweep through the heart muscle. Each normal beat gives a P wave (atria depolarising), a sharp QRS complex (ventricles depolarising, which hides atrial repolarisation) and a rounded T wave (ventricles repolarising). Rhythm diagnosis is largely pattern-reading of these landmarks. A normal trace has one P before every QRS at regular spacing. AV block stretches the P–Q interval or drops QRS complexes after some P waves; in complete block P waves and QRS complexes march independently. Bradycardia and tachycardia keep the normal shape but change the spacing between beats. Atrial fibrillation shows no true P waves, only a wobbling baseline, with irregularly spaced but normal-shaped QRS complexes. Ventricular fibrillation is a chaotic scrawl with no recognisable P, QRS or T. Tortora's Figure 20.24 shows normal, first-degree block, AF, VT and VF; it has no bradycardia or tachycardia strip.

basics: 'Failure' here means the heart cannot pump out all the blood it receives at a normal filling pressure. Blood then piles up behind the failing chamber, and where it piles up depends on which side fails. Behind the left ventricle are the lungs: raised pulmonary capillary pressure forces fluid into the alveoli (pulmonary oedema, breathlessness). Behind the right ventricle are the systemic veins: raised venous pressure forces fluid into tissues, giving swollen ankles and fluid in the abdomen (ascites) and a congested liver. The left side usually fails from ischaemia, infarction or years of pumping against high blood pressure; the right side fails from lung disease or a left-to-right shunt that raises pulmonary pressure (cor pulmonale), or simply because the left side failed first. A vicious circle follows: low output starves the kidneys, which respond as if to haemorrhage by releasing renin, so angiotensin and aldosterone retain salt and water, worsening congestion. Diuretics and ACE inhibitors interrupt this loop.

basics: This diagram summarises where the consequences of a failing pump show up, so read it as two chains of cause and effect. Forward (low output) effects: less blood to muscles gives fatigue and exercise intolerance; less to the kidneys triggers renin release, salt-and-water retention and a rising blood volume that the heart cannot handle. Backward (congestion) effects: left-ventricular failure raises left-atrial and pulmonary-vein pressure, pushing fluid into the lungs, so the patient is breathless, worse lying flat, and may cough frothy fluid; right-ventricular failure raises pressure in the venae cavae, so the neck veins distend, the liver swells, fluid collects in the abdomen and gravity pools it in the ankles. The heart itself dilates as end-diastolic volume climbs; stretching helps at first (Frank–Starling) but an over-stretched ventricle contracts more weakly, closing a positive-feedback loop. Tortora describes both sides of failure, the preload loop and oedema; ascites and neck-vein signs are the lecturer's additions.

basics: Venous blood pressure is low, only a few mmHg, and in the legs it must climb against gravity to the heart. Veins manage this with one-way valves, folds of the inner lining that close on any backflow, and with the skeletal-muscle pump that squeezes blood upward each time the calf contracts. The deep leg veins, wrapped in muscle, do most of the work; the thin-walled superficial veins under the skin drain into them through connecting veins with their own valves. If a valve leaks (from birth, ageing, or after stretching by a clot or long-standing high pressure), blood falls back and pools below it, distending the vein; a distended vein pulls its next valve cusps apart, so the fault spreads downward, a positive-feedback loop. The result is a swollen, tortuous varicose vein. Pregnancy, obesity and standing all raise leg venous pressure. Treatment supports the vein from outside (compression stockings), reduces the load, or destroys it (sclerotherapy scars the lining shut).

A blood clot forming in a deep vein of the leg; can damage valves and embolise to the lungs.
Injecting an irritant solution into a vein so it scars and closes.
Elastic stockings that squeeze the leg to stop blood pooling in superficial veins.

note: Tortora lists the same causes and treatments (p.779); DVT as a cause of varicose veins is not stated there, only defined in Medical Terminology (p.842).
